description: A random sample of reuse rows from both editions (seed 20261117): per edition 160 rows at status match and 40 at status possible, commonplaces left out. Claude Opus read each row (the edition passage with 350 characters of context on each side, the source passage, and the working French of a Latin source) and gave a verdict: right (the relation the label claims holds), weak (the passages treat the same point, but nothing specific shows that the edition draws on this source), wrong (the passages do not match). It also said whether the label fits. Where a source transcription was in the repository, the readers checked the source passage in context. The rows themselves are unchanged. rightCI95 and wrongCI95 are Wilson 95% intervals in per cent.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 711 says fair peace terms follow from the cause of war and the costs the declaring party was forced to incur; Vattel lists the same two parts: the principal subject plus reimbursement of preparation costs.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Wolff's § 135 in deriving love of country from the citizen's undertaking to promote the common good, after the self-love step.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's general principle renders Wolff's: a nation owes another what it owes itself, insofar as the other needs it and it can give it without neglecting its duties to itself.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific rule as Wolff: a peace treaty may include stipulations unrelated to the war only if they are expressly stated.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's sentence on individual natural law being modified when applied to states paraphrases Wolff's earlier 'illis convenienter immutanda sunt'; this source sentence is about modifying the natural law of nations into the voluntary law, a different point.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same rule from Grotius III.20.7: the loser is compensated 'des deniers publics' and citizens contribute by proportion if needed.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: That the sovereign may compel subjects to be hostages is a stock Grotian point, and the wording differs too much for a close paraphrase.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: Vattel's quoted preface renders Wolff's sentence on natural and necessary law of nations word for word.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both give the specific rule that when a river abandons its bed entirely, the old bed stays the boundary between the two states.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's solution, that the released prisoner keeps his liberty but pays a just equivalent, is Grotius III.xxi.30's solution to the same case.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's statement that the form of the republic makes no difference to what belongs to the nation is his argument on precedence (it stands in § 243, not § 153), which Vattel restates.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel reproduces Wolff's two steps: perfection as the accord of a thing's parts toward one end, and the nation as a multitude united in civil society.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument: excluding one people from what is permitted to all foreigners is an injury, unless it is punishment for a crime.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Punish or deliver up at the offended sovereign's request is Grotius's maxim (II.21.4), which Burlamaqui copies; nothing ties Vattel to Burlamaqui, and Vattel's wording differs too much for a close paraphrase.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: 'Natural law applied to nations' is a stock formula that Vattel's preface traces to Hobbes and Pufendorf; nothing ties this sentence to Burlamaqui in particular.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument (an armed ambassador may be resisted by natural self-defence) with the same example of the Roman ambassadors fighting the Gauls at Clusium.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's maxim that neither party may interpret the treaty at will is Wolff's rule for treaties, with the same two-sided reasoning.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The division into personal and real alliances, the personal expiring with the contractor, is stock doctrine (Grotius, Pufendorf, Wolff); nothing ties Vattel to Pufendorf's wording.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's view of Saguntum, that Carthage could act against a Roman ally on just cause without breaking the treaty, follows Barbeyrac's note in its wording.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The excuse for non-performance by necessity sits in a similar place in the peace-treaty chapters, but it rests on the commonplace that no one is bound to the impossible, and Vattel's elaboration is not in Grotius.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel renders Wolff's paired definition of postliminy for persons and things falling back into their nation's power.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument in the same order: milder means must be preferred while they suffice, reprisals are milder than war, and they must be used while they can obtain redress.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both hold that the sovereign who breaks faith cannot make hostages answer for it with their lives, and the next row shows both go on to make the hostage a mere prisoner.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's third rule on favourable things (no improper sense except to avoid absurdity or nullity) follows Pufendorf's numbered rules 2-3 in the same order and structure.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same rule and wording: respect due to the character, and in doubt whether goods belong to the minister's person, 'on explique toujours les choses' in his favour.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both state the same conflict-of-laws rule, that a precept yields where it cannot be done without breaking a prohibition (moral impossibility), and illustrate it with theft for charity.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's two kinds of reasons follow Wolff's definitions (justificatory reasons from right, suasive ones from utility, each 'by which it is shown').

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Both state the same Wolffian rule (obscure or equivocal wording explained by clearer wording elsewhere), but Vattel recasts the main clause ('il est le meilleur interprete de lui-même').

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's limit on offices to other nations ('sans manquer à ses devoirs envers elle-même') reproduces Wolff's 'citra neglectum officii erga se ipsam'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's sentence states the standard rule that only the sovereign makes a general truce, worded and argued after Wolff JG § 932; nothing ties it to Pufendorf's own short-truce formulation.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel takes up the case for poisoned weapons and declares them forbidden by natural law, against Wolff's claim that they are not naturally illicit.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note on Bynkershoek makes the same inference about Rincon and Fregoso: Charles V's neglect to seek the murderers shows he at least approved the deed after the fact.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific case (freed prisoner retaken before paying owes the first ransom and a second), but in different wording and sentence form.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's claim that foreign nations may not judge between prince and subjects, grounded on non-interference, renders Wolff 1011.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Within the same favourable/odious sequence as Pufendorf V.12.12 (equality, burdens on one party), Vattel gives the Quintilian rule in nearly Barbeyrac's words.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same rule that a treaty made for the contractor and his successors is real, not personal; the wording and structure differ.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'participe à l'action de son sujet & s'en charge' renders Wolff's ruler who 'concurrit ad factum civis', turning the subject's act into the nation's act.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument that ceding uncultivated land to incoming settlers is both a benefit to them and a gain in population and power for the nation.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That the only just cause of war is an injury done or threatened is a Grotian commonplace; the two texts share only the maxim.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel restates Wolff § 338's thesis that a nation keeps some right over another's property when deprived of a necessary use, clause by clause.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'répugne en soi à tout traité de protection' renders Wolff's 'foederi omni protectionis per se inest', and the bar on aiding the protector's enemies follows from it.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's maxim translates Wolff's 'quod sufficienter significatur, id contra ipsum pro vero habetur' word for word, though Wolff applies it to war here.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Wolff's sequence: enrolling another's subjects is plagium, soldiers swear an oath, deserters are severely punished, and those who promote desertion share the plagium.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel copies and cites Grotius II.15.5 for this division of treaties; Pufendorf only restates the same Grotian division, so nothing points to him.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Wolff's note in sequence: what holds of soldiers holds of subordinate officers, who are like private persons, military law forbids acting without orders, and war's outcomes are uncertain.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific argument: an oath cannot give a later ally priority over an earlier ally whose treaty is unsworn.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note defines civil war in republics as two opposed parties in arms and distinguishes rebellion and rival pretenders, as Vattel does.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The rule that a treaty with a republic is real is stock. Vattel's 'toute alliance ... réelle de sa nature' matches Pufendorf VIII.ix.6 more closely than Burlamaqui's 'tout traité'.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Booty belonging to the warring sovereign, whoever takes it, is standard doctrine, and Vattel's wording (soldiers and auxiliaries as instruments) follows Wolff JG §§ 852-854; the wording is not close to Pufendorf's.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel rejects the view that 'the manner is indifferent' and condemns poison as contrary to natural law, against Wolff's claim (§§877-878) that killing the enemy by poison is naturally licit.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Both texts give the same first condition of reprisals (the wrong or debt must be evident), followed by the prior demand for justice, but in different words.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same rule with the same opening construction: once a custom is established among nations it binds them by their tacit consent.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific example: the widow's statutory portion cannot be reduced when a citizen makes his will abroad.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel restates Wolff 322: a later occupant of a vacant country cannot take the places or rights already occupied by another nation.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The rule that the receiving power cannot punish an ambassador is stock doctrine, and Vattel gives a different ground (independence) from Barbeyrac's (he represents his master).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's proposition that a nation may be punished by taking corporeal things and rights is what Vattel restates (things, rights, towns, provinces taken as punishment).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel repeats Grotius's verdict on the Ansibarii example (the maxim is sound but misapplied because the Romans used the land), with a different use.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both Vattel texts ground the measure of penalties in their end, to secure the safety of citizens and state, in shared wording.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific argument that a sea enclosed in a nation's lands can be appropriated like land, as Grotius argues in II.3.10.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel uses Wolff's specific analogy of two disputants over the truth of a proposition to show war cannot be just on both sides.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel reproduces Wolff's rule that, since parties cannot be presumed to have meant to do nothing, an interpretation voiding the act is not admitted.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Vattel names Pufendorf (note 'Ibid.' to DNG II.3.23) as subscribing to Hobbes's view, echoing 'je souscris absolument'.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Vattel follows Grotius III.20.26 ('il pouvoit s'expliquer plus clairement; s'il ne l'a pas fait, tant pis pour lui') and then quotes the same Digest maxim that Grotius gives in his note.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff 504-505 lets a hostage be retained as a debtor for debts contracted while held, without breaching the release; Vattel states the same rule and adds crimes.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's argument that the war is not the auxiliaries' so booty is not theirs, with the same 'no difficulty' remark and the next point that the sovereign disposes of booty.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Vattel's note on those who rejected the favourable/odious distinction sends to Barbeyrac's remarks on Grotius, which is this note rejecting that distinction.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both say a state makes the citizen's act its own by approving or ratifying it; same Wolffian doctrine and key terms.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel quotes Pufendorf's two rules almost word for word, citing VIII.9.8, and dismisses them as beside the question.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The power-plus-will condition comes from Grotius II.22.5 and is common stock; nothing in Vattel's wording points to Burlamaqui's Droit politique rather than Grotius.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel corrects the view that the law of nations is just natural law with nations put in place of individuals, a view his preface ascribes to Pufendorf II.3.23 following Hobbes.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's refusal to distinguish major from minor articles, since breach of the least article frees the other party, is Wolff § 1024's rule that peace is broken even by violating minor articles.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Grotius's argument that courts replaced private war and echoes Paul's maxim as Barbeyrac renders it ('on ne doit pas souffrir que les particuliers...').

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Taking passage by force when it is unjustly refused is the common Grotius-Pufendorf-Wolff doctrine, and nothing in the wording ties Vattel's sentence to Pufendorf in particular.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The conditional formula is Grotius's: Vattel names Grotius and matches Grotius-Barbeyrac word for word, while Pufendorf's version reverses the clauses.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's ruler, holding the nation's rights, represents his nation in its dealings, which Vattel states as the sovereign's representative character.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same rule of interpretation: words take their common-usage sense unless there is strong reason (conjecture) otherwise.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific point as Barbeyrac's note: when ratification has been reserved, it is understood as an express ratification.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel gives Wolff's specific reason why a father's safe-conduct excludes wife and children (they do not usually travel with him) but recasts it with a contrast to permission to settle.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's note restates Grotius's note on Horace's ode, that Achilles would not shut himself in the famous horse, and quotes the same lines.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same exception to presumed abandonment: fear or another impediment prevented the owner from speaking.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel answers Grotius II.2.13 with the two points of Barbeyrac's note on it: passage is not strictly owed except in extreme necessity, and its innocence cannot be presumed.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius's point that those who equip ships and act against the enemy at their own expense get the captures as reward is restated for privateers with parallel structure.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel renders Wolff's Prolegomena §4 closely: necessary law of nations contains what natural law prescribes to nations, binding them as it binds men.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The rule that the public compensates individuals whose goods are disposed of by eminent domain is common stock (Grotius, Pufendorf); Wolff states it generally, not for peace treaties.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's definition of retorsion of right renders Wolff's definition closely.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'since the truce cannot bind subjects unless known, it must be published' restates Wolff's inference that subjects are bound only after publication (also in Grotius III.21.5).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both are about a sovereign keeping faith with rebels: a settlement or amnesty means the whole past is pardoned or forgotten, so the prince must keep his word.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument: treaties merely not to harm are unnecessary among civilised peoples but needed where foreigners are treated as fair game (Pufendorf's ancients, Vattel's barbarians).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel grounds postliminy, as Wolff § 894 does, in the sovereign's duty to defend subjects, with restitution of persons to all their rights and goods to their owners.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same thesis, that a prince abroad may exercise sovereign acts over his own subjects but not territorial jurisdiction, and Vattel's examples follow; the sentence structure differs, so it is a loose paraphrase.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same sequence of duties: give each his right, repair the injury, give satisfaction for the irreparable one, give security where faith is suspect.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's definition of equal treaties includes Pufendorf's proportional member ('à proportion des forces' / 'équitablement proportionnées') and the same troop and ship examples.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both state Wolff's general voluntary-law principle that natural liberty leaves each nation to its own judgment, but Inst. 1215 applies it to the justice of both sides in war, not to trying peaceful means first.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument as Wolff: a sovereign who will not punish or make restitution for private breaches takes part in them and himself violates the faith of the truce.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Religion's effect on society giving the sovereign authority over it is the common jus circa sacra argument, and the wording is different.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's treaties fixing 'ce qui ne peut être déterminé en général par le droit naturel' render Wolff § 392's 'quae jure naturali in genere determinata non sunt' in a treaty context.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Vattel copies Barbeyrac's French rendering of Aristotle on unequal friendship word for word, in the same discussion of unequal alliances.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same Wolffian prohibition on hindering another nation from attaining the end of civil society, with near-identical structure.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific argument: a safe-conduct granted at pleasure lapses on the grantor's death because he ceases to will.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both treat corrupting the enemy's garrison as a breach of truce, a specific Grotian rule that Vattel widens to governors and subjects.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf VIII.1.6 gives the same argument: in doubtful cases subjects presume the sovereign's orders just and may not examine them, and the guilt falls on the commander.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf's specific rule that a treaty for the king's or his family's personal advantage ends with his death or the family's extinction (absent from Wolff) is restated, but in a compressed sentence, not the same structure.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel restates Wolff's two conditions for offices of humanity (the other's need, and no neglect of duty to oneself) and goes on, as Wolff § 157 does, to the asked nation's right to judge and the grain example.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific argument that necessity entitles a belligerent to seize war goods sent to his enemy by others.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel translates exactly the Cicero excerpt that Grotius quotes, from 'At quid interest' to 'consuerunt', in the same argument that one's word binds as much as an oath, so the relation is translation.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel gives Wolff's two rules: whoever is granted passage repairs the damage, and the ruler sees that the injured subjects are compensated.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same rule for war manifestos with the same list of words to avoid (hatred, animosity, a third violent passion), in parallel structure.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: Vattel's preface quotes Wolff's preface in French: the opening sentence on nations using only natural law, so a separate treatise may seem superfluous.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same eminent-domain rule with the same wording 'dédommager des deniers publics', followed by all citizens contributing.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The rule that foreigners' offences are punished under local law is a standard maxim, and the wording does not match beyond 'suivant les loix du pays/lieu'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel reproduces the argument Pufendorf gives (after Grotius) in this paragraph: freedom to buy or not means no right to sell goods to an unwilling people.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's definition of pactions as agreements with transitory, non-repeated performances renders Wolff's definition.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel moves Grotius's truce rule (parties bound at conclusion, subjects only from notification) over to the peace treaty, saying explicitly that it is the same as for the truce.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The Procopius anecdote of the Goth and the Roman soldier is told word for word as in Barbeyrac's Pufendorf.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Near-translation of Wolff's rule that a ransom agreement cannot be rescinded because the captive proves richer than believed.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same rule: if a power shows designs of domination and does even the slightest injury, the other nations may join to weaken it by arms.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's sentence is a word-for-word rendering of Wolff's Latin, so 'translation' fits better than 'close paraphrase'.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: Vattel's definition of the droit d'aubaine translates Wolff's definition of jus albinagii clause by clause.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Same phrase in Vattel's own Questions, on the same point that the prince does best to entrust justice to a company of wise, upright and enlightened judges.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same threefold division of ways a peace treaty is broken (essence of any peace, particular nature of this peace, express articles) with shared wording, order varied.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Both say that some pre-war debts survive a peace treaty, but Burlamaqui follows Grotius III.20.16 on private debts suspended by war, while Vattel is about claims unrelated to the war's causes; different rules, different wording.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Grotius here assigns acquisitions (including those by war) to an arbitrary law of nations distinct from natural law, which is the attribution Vattel names and rejects.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel extends to unjustly conquered peoples the duty in conscience to restore what is recovered from an unjust enemy, following Grotius III.16 (cited at § 196) and its § IV.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel restates Barbeyrac's specific argument that nations have no interest in whether private persons act without orders, so the rule belongs to public law rather than the law of nations.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: In his conflict rules, which follow Pufendorf V.12.23, Vattel takes Barbeyrac's note that the later of two opposed conventions prevails, other things being equal.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same Wolffian argument that private war is not tolerated because judges render each his right, applied to the duel.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's definition of domicile renders Wolff's Latin definition word for word.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's definition of consuls follows Wolff's clause by clause: ports, commission, guarding the nation's rights and privileges, settling merchants' disputes.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That peace restores nations to their natural state follows from the common view that peace is the natural state; the wording overlap is slight.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Grotius II.16.25 (tacit condition rebus sic stantibus) and gives a named instance (Titus) of Grotius's envoys who turned back; same example type, but not the same content words.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Near-translation of Wolff's rule that matters on which the peace treaty is silent remain as they are.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific explanation: hostages were once killed through the error that a man has a right over his own life or that the sovereign may dispose of it.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 631: in a doubtful cause war is lawful only to force a party that refuses accommodation into a transaction; Vattel gives the same rule, then Wolff's § 632 point that war does not decide right.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel renders Wolff's definition of the perfection of a nation and of its perfect state almost clause for clause.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's clause renders Wolff's proposition that a nation must love itself nearly word for word, so it is closer than a loose paraphrase.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both concern a balance in which joined weaker powers offset the preponderant one, but Wolff's definition has none of Vattel's scale image or coalition practice.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Sparing old men, women and children is the common Grotian temperamentum; the wording and grounds differ, since Vattel rests it on their offering no resistance.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'tant qu'il ne l'est pas expressément [révoqué], il demeure valable' gives Barbeyrac's point that the clause keeps the safe-conduct in force until clearly revoked, but in different words and structure.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Grotius-Barbeyrac's wording that tribute, as an admission of weakness, diminishes something of the state's dignity but leaves sovereignty intact.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: Vattel translates Wolff's definition of jura merae facultatis almost word for word (use or not use as one pleases, free of all constraint).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel cites Grotius's note and restates its report that French ordinances let the French seize such goods and keep them on paying their value.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Vattel's footnote names Grotius III.20.55 on hostages, the source locus given.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's definition of inferior powers, with magistrates and generals as examples, translates Wolff's closely.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Refusing obedience to commands evidently contrary to natural law is, as Vattel himself says, the view of all authors; nothing specific ties the passage to the Questions remark.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Same Livy quotation of Camillus used for the same three just causes of war (defence, recovery, punishment) as in Grotius II.i.2 and Barbeyrac's note.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Vattel's note names Grotius on tacit conventions made by mute signs, which is Grotius III.24.5.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note gives the same reasons Vattel uses: general and long truces are too consequential for a general, and among the Romans long truces needed the Senate and People.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's Scipio sentence follows Barbeyrac's wording (déclaré hautement, innocent hostages, only armed enemies), and his note cites this Grotius section.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel and Formey give the same rule in the same order: a term to leave, enemy treatment after it, and a delay for an insurmountable obstacle such as illness.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's account of writers who give the name of law of nations to certain usages binding by consent echoes Pufendorf II.3.23, the paragraph he discusses later in the same preface.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's Scipio declaration (no revenge on innocent hostages, only on armed enemies) follows Barbeyrac's French closely, for the same point.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's sentence renders Wolff's thesis of par. 263 closely: no nation may refuse the offices of humanity to another because of a different religion.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Both say that after a long truce that has removed 'tout l'appareil' of war, a declaration before resuming arms is fitting though not strictly required.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The same Antiochus example ends with the identical clause 'les fit tous scier par le milieu', in Pufendorf's sequence (Plataeans, the Roman, Rhadamistus smothered).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's sentence renders Wolff's 'nothing wins nations and their rulers more praise than entire good faith' in the same comparative structure.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 501: only the hostage's liberty is pledged, not his life, and the old contrary opinion assumed a right over one's own life; Vattel gives the same thesis and correction.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's limit of sea dominion to what a nation needs for security and can make respected restates Wolff § 128 (occupation as far as dominion can be defended, the sea as a rampart).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The truce defined as suspending hostilities without ending the war is the stock Grotian definition; nothing ties Vattel's recall to Burlamaqui's wording.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Vattel's sentence closely follows Esprit des loix XXVI.23 (a succession order destructive of the state may be changed by a new law), but he names Montesquieu only in the next section, I.62.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's specific rule that during a truce the besieged may not repair the rampart breached by enemy guns is restated by Vattel, with an echo of the enemy artillery.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel denies a besieged governor the right to repair breaches during a truce, against the general permission that comes from Grotius III.21.7; nothing aims the correction at Burlamaqui in particular.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both deny that usages bind universally, but Vattel's sentence translates Wolff Prol. § 24, and Burlamaqui's point (usages not obligatory by themselves) differs in substance.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both ground the safety of envoys between belligerents in the duty to seek means of restoring peace, with shared wording (devoir, moyens, retablir la paix).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The shared phrase 'prétend avoir le droit de son côté' and the Wolffian voluntary-law argument are general; Formey states the rule for belligerents, Vattel applies it to a deposed king, so nothing ties the two passages specifically.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The definition of an equal alliance as one where neither party is inferior is stock; Vattel's own treaty/alliance distinction is not in Pufendorf's passage.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both mention public goods for the sovereign's upkeep and state expenses, but Burlamaqui distinguishes royal domain from public treasury while Vattel's point is that taxes are reserved to the nation; a commonplace overlap.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Grotius III.22.7-8: a general cannot make peace but can make conventions binding only himself and his troops.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both state the stock Wolffian thesis that peace treaties are real and bind successors, but in different words and with different arguments.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The maxim that self-government is the mark of independence is general. Vattel II.57's own point, the right to repel interference, is not in Wolff § 256.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That an owner may alienate or pledge what is its own is a stock consequence of dominion, and Wolff §484 on what nations may pledge has none of Vattel's specific argument.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both deny binding force to grossly unjust imposed treaties, a Grotius-Barbeyrac commonplace; Vattel's naming of true peace treaties is not a restatement of Burlamaqui's clause.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Formey's 'C'est encore un droit particulier' (customary law, after conventional law) shares Vattel's Wolffian classification in the same words, which is verbatim rather than loose paraphrase.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Equal conduct toward both belligerents is the general neutrality rule; Grotius limits it to doubtful wars, Vattel makes it unconditional, and nothing specific ties his sentence to this passage.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both concern inducing a garrison to surrender by threat rather than killing those who yield, but Grotius advises the threat of the sword, which Vattel rejects in favour of a threat of no capitulation.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both concern not refusing enemy envoys, but Wolff speaks only of manifest necessity such as peace offers, while Vattel's general maxim and its exceptions are not in this passage.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel takes up Pufendorf's specific point that the will of a lawgiver or contracting party may rest on several reasons, so the failure of one need not end the law, and develops it at more length.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific episode, the Spanish ambassador's secretary arrested with Mairargues, used in the same context of ambassadors' staff caught in a plot.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same sequence as Wolff 875-876: non-resisting enemies are not to be harmed, so commanders must not permit soldiers to rape women and girls.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's sovereign who wages wars without reason and disturbs public tranquillity is the Wolffian disturber of public peace that Formey defines.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both state a general duty of states to promote other states' good as far as they can, but Vattel's Wolffian 'bonheur et perfection' formula has no specific link to Burlamaqui's passage.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel uses Barbeyrac's specific argument that ambassadorial safety must not override the safety of the receiving sovereign, in the same debate over punishing a plotting ambassador.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both reason from a presumed intention to abandon flooded land, but Vattel reaches the opposite presumption for a large area between states, so this is not a paraphrase.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel names Wicquefort for sovereigns who only expelled plotting ambassadors, the practice the dedication states; it is a reference, not a paraphrase.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That the ruler should protect the sciences and arts is a general maxim; Wolff's definitional sentence gives nothing specific to Vattel's passage.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The idea that without consent or lawful government the state of war continues after conquest is common stock; Burlamaqui's clause itself copies Barbeyrac's note on Grotius, and Vattel's condition differs.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That an agent acting within his commission binds the principal is the general rule of mandate, which Vattel invokes as such; Grotius's passage concerns subordinate powers.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That treaties made with the state itself bind successors is the stock Grotian definition of real treaties; Vattel refers back to his own II § 189.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both hold the hostage liable for his own acts, but Wolff's section 533 concerns his personal suretyship for the main obligation, not crimes and private debts during hostageship (Wolff section 505).

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Grounding the perfect/imperfect right distinction in natural liberty is Vattel's (and Wolff's) standing doctrine; the §904 remark shares no wording or example with the buying case.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's rule that a command yields to a prohibition because the prohibition binds absolutely and the precept only when the occasion allows is Grotius's second conflict rule and its reason (II.16.29), reworded.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's section is about the ruler's freedom to admit a foreigner as citizen or resident, not a definition of inhabitants; it overlaps with Vattel's only in the idea of allowing a foreigner to reside.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: 'Opposer la force à quiconque' attacks one's rights is a stock statement of the right of defence; Burlamaqui uses it as an example of perfect rights.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both say peace is broken by violating treaty articles, a stock Grotian definition with nothing specific to these two texts.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel rejects the patrimonial-state notion and, in the next section, names Grotius's alienations; this contradicts Grotius's claim that a king holding the realm as patrimony may alienate it.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Conspiring against or favouring a plot against the state as grounds for acting against an ambassador is common doctrine; the shared verb pair is too slight to show reliance on Burlamaqui.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: In the same Rosny-case discussion, Barbeyrac's note on Bynkershoek says jurisdiction over the household depends on the will of the ambassador's master, which is Vattel's point.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both treat fear as a bar to a presumption of abandonment drawn from silence, but Vattel reverses Grotius's point and shares no wording, so it is not a paraphrase.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's passage is about taxes supplementing an insufficient domain; the source passage distinguishes goods for the king's upkeep from goods for state expenses.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same rule that movables count as taken once safely out of pursuit, valid against neutral third parties, in the same sequence.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both render Wolff's argument that the common welfare of nations requires secure, inviolable treaties and that this has nothing to do with religion.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same inference that because society needs mutual benevolence, God wills men to have these sentiments, in parallel wording.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The two sentences are identical except for 'd'une' ('Tel est premierement l'état de l'homme par rapport à Dieu, qui est un état de dépendance absolue').

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Nearly identical sentence frame: 'quand il s'agit de déterminer précisément jusqu'... on doit imputer une action à quelcun'.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's sentence repeats Barbeyrac's note almost word for word ('chose également absurde & funeste à la Société, que de prétendre que ... subsiste toujours ... inconvéniens').

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui follows Pufendorf's Archytas sentence closely: occasional lapses do not make a man vicious, nor a single good act a good man, with shared phrasing (mettre au rang des, se sont laissé aller, gens de bien).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same sentence that men cannot do without one another's help, in the same argument on the natural state of society.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui reuses his own definitional sentence ('c'est le système ou l'assemblage de ces lois... que l'on appelle') nearly word for word for the law of nations; it is the same wording, not the same content in other words.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's treatment of forced actions follows Pufendorf's first kind of constraint, irresistible physical violence, which excuses the agent.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui repeats Pufendorf's sentence that every obligation supposes reasons acting on conscience so that we judge resistance wrong, nearly word for word.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Burlamaqui gives the Roman-law rule on the unborn in exactly Barbeyrac's French wording (censés/censez only).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's three principles (religion, self-love, sociability) from three relations of man are Barbeyrac's derivation in this note.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both Burlamaqui texts argue that power gives a right to command only if reason approves it, so a malevolent power gives none.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Both texts give the same French rendering of Seneca word for word ('Autant d'hommes, autant de proyes et de victimes').

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The jurists' threefold fault (gross, light, very light) is a Roman-law commonplace, and Burlamaqui justifies it differently from Pufendorf's three degrees of care.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Note (a) names Grotius I.1 §§ 4-7, which holds the perfect/imperfect division of rights the section goes on to give.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The Principes and the Élémens share the statement that subsequent conscience is tranquil or uneasy in nearly the same words.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note that even those not subject to the laws should praise or blame actions by their conformity to them, in the same imputation context.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The definition of the subaltern cause is Barbeyrac's note almost word for word.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Both make the author of the compulsion the sole author of the act and the compelled agent a mere passive instrument.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui reworks Barbeyrac's preface sentence: ideas of order and convenance, 'fait de tout tems impression sur les hommes' among somewhat civilised nations, confused sentiment, acquiescence.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same list of the soul's principal faculties (understanding, will, liberty) in nearly the same words.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's note pointing to Matthew XV.4-5 as another example, after the exposure of children by Greeks and Romans, comes from Barbeyrac's Devoirs note, which pairs the same two errors.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui takes Barbeyrac's argument and wording: 'de cela seul que l'on veut du bien à quelqu'un, il ne s'ensuit pas' that one has a right to command.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same example, worded nearly the same ('les Grecs & les Romains ... qu'il étoit permis à un Père d'exposer ses enfans'), used as a moral error, from Barbeyrac's note on the Devoirs chapter Burlamaqui follows.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note gives the three principles (religion, self-love, sociability) as linked but distinct and concurring in the Creator's views, which Burlamaqui restates.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui reuses the terms of Barbeyrac's note ('précise & immédiate' versus 'condition nécessairement supposée') on the Devoirs passage he cites (I.2.4).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The third rule of conscience follows Barbeyrac's note nearly word for word ('on se laisse aller tranquillement...').

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Same definition of human actions as those produced and directed by 'ces nobles facultez dont le Créateur a enrichi l'homme', word for word from Barbeyrac's Devoirs I.i.2.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Burlamaqui names Pufendorf, reports his point in nearly his words ('autorisée par une tradition très-ancienne... Divinité Vengeresse') and cites DNG II.3.21 in note (b).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same opening of the sanction chapter: the force of laws depends on sanction, so one must ask whether natural laws carry penalties and rewards, in nearly the same words.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The three proofs of God's existence (subordination of causes, first mover, order of the universe) are copied clause for clause.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same syllogism from direction, end and happiness to the definition of droit, nearly word for word.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Burlamaqui endorses Barbeyrac's claim ('on a remarqué avec raison') in nearly the same sentence frame; he rejects Grotius, not this note.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's Devoirs note says that human laws draw their force from divine natural law, a different point; Burlamaqui's sentence comes from Barbeyrac's note 6 on DJNG I.6.18.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The note prints Cicero's Latin from Tusc. I.32-33 word for word.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui follows Pufendorf's two parts of a law and the reason that a command without a threat is useless, but in different wording and with his own 'counsel' conclusion.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's argument that it is not beyond human firmness to die rather than fail one's duty, with people doing so for light reasons, is taken nearly word for word.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both define the right/straight as the shortest path to the end by the metaphor of the straight line, Cumberland's specific teleological analogy, which Burlamaqui applies to 'règle'.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Burlamaqui cites Devoirs I.1 §17 and faults Pufendorf for not separating imputability from actual imputation, as Barbeyrac's note does.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: In a passage that cites Barbeyrac's remarks on the Jugement d'un anonyme, Burlamaqui uses Barbeyrac's formula of the will 'de laquelle on se reconnoît dépendant'.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Burlamaqui quotes Grotius's definition of natural law in Barbeyrac's translation word for word, naming Grotius.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui takes Barbeyrac's three principles (religion, self-love, sociability) with self-love as the ground of duties to oneself, but he rewords the sentence.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same fourfold division of rights in the same order and names (liberty, property or domain, empire or authority, rights over others' things) as Pufendorf I.1.19.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui follows Barbeyrac's note: demonstrative conscience rests on demonstrative reasons as far as moral matters allow, and probable conscience rests only on likelihoods.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Burlamaqui names Grotius and rejects his claim of a voluntary positive divine law given to all mankind (I.1.15).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's definition of natural law reproduces Pufendorf's 'convient si ... à la nature ... de l'Homme, que sans l'observation de ces maximes' construction.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same fundamental principle of imputability, with 'pour dire la même chose en d'autres termes', 'l'existence ou la non-existence' and the converse clause taken from Pufendorf I.5.5.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Near-verbatim same conclusion that all free actions are voluntary but not all voluntary actions free.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same sentence frame and wording: to judge these two characters one must look at the whole course of life, not single moments.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's sentence on the Roman jurists' first sense of jus gentium copies Barbeyrac's note word for word.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf's sentence continues with the same principle and the same rephrasing ('pour dire la même chose en d'autres termes... soumise à la direction... mise sur le compte'), which Burlamaqui reproduces.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both give the stock definition of morality as the relation of actions to law; the edition sentence only recaps Part I ch. XI, so nothing ties this passage specifically to the Élémens sentence.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same inference as Barbeyrac's Reflexions: God, author of the nature of things and of reason, thereby wills that we conform our conduct to it, with the shared phrase 'Auteur de la nature des choses'.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui equates voluntary ignorance with vincible error contracted by negligence, as Pufendorf does, but defines it in a different sentence structure.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Burlamaqui quotes Barbeyrac's argument (reason is only ourselves, so the maxims of reason do not oblige) and declares it insufficient.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The note prints Seneca's Attalus saying verbatim, under a slightly wrong letter number.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's 'simple' imputation (approval or blame with no further effect on the agent) recasts Pufendorf's point that the approval or blame of those without authority touches only the agent's reputation.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's conditions for a good action (knowledge, and the intention 'de rendre à la Loi l'obéissance' it is owed, with a vicious intention making it imputable as bad) follow Pufendorf I.7.4 closely.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's two-legislators argument for the greater efficacy of penalties than rewards is taken over closely.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui copies Barbeyrac's note word for word ('peut bien diminuer le crime de celui qui commet, quoi que malgré soi, une action mauvaise, contre les lumiéres de sa Conscience'), inserting one clause.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The clause 'la nécessité d'agir ou de ne point agir d'une certaine manière' comes word for word from Barbeyrac's note, used in the same argument that permission is a positive effect of law.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument from our inclination to good and aversion to evil, in the parallel chapter, but in different words and sentence form (rhetorical questions).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The Élémens editor reports Burlamaqui's Avertissement on publishing this first part, uncertain whether the rest would follow, in near-identical words in the third person.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui reproduces Barbeyrac's concession that sociability is the widest principle but the other two keep their own independent force, nearly word for word.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Near-verbatim same transitional sentence: man acts only for happiness, but can reach it only by reason.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument from Pufendorf I.8.1: good actions admit no degrees, while bad ones are more or less vicious, like curved lines departing more or less from the straight line.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vincible error is defined as error avoidable 'si l'on eût pris tous les soins', in Pufendorf's wording and structure.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same definition of moeurs as free actions considered as susceptible of rules, in nearly the same words.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Near-identical phrase: dispositions do not 'porter invinciblement les hommes a violer' the natural law, making the same point.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui follows Pufendorf's sentence: laws are seldom broken except in hope of an apparent good, so the best counter is the threat of pain.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Note (b) to P2.9.5 names Barbeyrac's note 1 on Devoirs I.1.5, the note that defines conscience and gives the same two rules Burlamaqui sets out.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both of Burlamaqui's texts grade an action's gravity by how noble its object is, in similar words ('objet... noble... criminelle').

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Burlamaqui quotes the Isocrates passage in exactly Barbeyrac's French wording from the note to Pufendorf II.3.21.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The Élémens share the PDN's 'droit as faculty' sense with the same father-educating-children example, in condensed form.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same definition of God ('c'est-à-dire, un premier Etre... de qui tout dépend'), followed in both by the proof from 'la subordination des Causes, qui demande'.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same sentence pattern: laws are not made 'proprement' to constrain subjects but 'plutôt' to make them act according to their true interests.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same definition of faculty as a power of acting, at the same point (list of the soul's faculties) in Burlamaqui's later Élémens.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Near-verbatim reuse of Barbeyrac's note: by degree of influence, the same acts make one a principal, collateral or subaltern cause.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The same rhetorical question appears almost word for word.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Only the commonplace end-means maxim is shared: Burlamaqui applies it to the agent's own will, Pufendorf to a legislator who prescribes an end.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's division of ignorance by its origin into voluntary and involuntary repeats Pufendorf's wording, within the same sequence of divisions.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's example of accidental error is copied word for word, dropping only 'sans le connoître'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: PDP restates Burlamaqui's own PDN doctrine that sovereignty rests on a power joined with goodness and wisdom (a 'puissance bienfaisante').

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same transition to droit taken as loi, with the same example and the clause 'dans tous ces cas le droit est pris pour la loi'.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Burlamaqui cites Pufendorf II.3.21, grants that reason gives only high probability on punishment after death, and rejects excluding the future state from natural law.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The phrase is word for word Barbeyrac's French rendering of the Cicero passage in Pufendorf III.3.1, which Burlamaqui quotes in the same wording.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both say the retrospective judgement of conscience produces either tranquillity or disquiet, together with the expectation of the legislator's favour.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Burlamaqui rejects Pufendorf's charge, made in II.iii.4, that Grotius's foundation of natural law in honest and dishonest acts is circular.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Pufendorf's thought experiment of a grown man raised alone, with the clause 'sans autre(s) connoissances que celles qu'il auroit acquises de lui-même' word for word.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui echoes the Devoirs sentence that the ideas of good and evil are not pure and simple, goods presenting themselves to us mixed with evils.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's definition of law as imposing obligation on some acts and leaving liberty in others follows Barbeyrac's note wording ('l'obligation de faire ou de ne pas faire certaines choses ... la liberté ... d'autres').

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same author, same chapter on God's existence: the denial of a Creator (chance or atheism) is called the greatest chimera or extravagance of the human mind.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's Cicero quotation reproduces Barbeyrac's French rendering in Pufendorf III.3.1, including the gloss 'c'est-à-dire, pour s'entr'aider'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui takes Barbeyrac's conditions for imputation: a connection between act and effect, and knowledge or foresight of it with some likelihood.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The figurative definition of a rule is word for word the same apart from the added 'une Maxime'.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Burlamaqui quotes the end of Grotius's definition of natural law word for word.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note says it is 'brouiller les idées' to make the useful the foundation of the honest, and Burlamaqui makes the same point with the same phrase.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Real versus apparent goods and their mixture is a commonplace, and Pufendorf uses it to explain differing natural inclinations, not as a rule of discernment.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both tie imputation to praise or blame and reward or punishment, but that pairing is stock; the Élémens' 'two manners' answers the PDN's simple/efficacious distinction (§ IX) more than this definition.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's Seneca quotation repeats Barbeyrac's French rendering, with the clause 'il n'y a que ce commerce de bienfaits qui rende la vie commode' identical.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The note prints Cicero's Latin from De Senectute 21 word for word.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's sentence that indifferent actions certainly exist, since many things are neither commanded nor forbidden by any law divine or human, is reproduced almost word for word.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The third rule of conscience copies Barbeyrac's sentence ('Supposé qu'en général on ait les lumières & les secours nécessaires pour juger...') nearly word for word.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's definition of imputability follows Pufendorf's sentence clause by clause (author, accountable, effects fall on him).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf II.3.13 is the source of Burlamaqui's sequence: natural law is 'known to all men' through reason, and innateness 'des le premier moment de notre existence' is 'une pure supposition'.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument from Barbeyrac's Réflexions against a positive law of nations: one is presumed to conform to a received usage unless one declares otherwise.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's division of states into primitive and accessory/adventitious follows Pufendorf's division of the moral state into natural and accessory.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Laws must be known to 'actuellement régler' men's 'mouvemens', put as the same rhetorical question as Pufendorf's.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Burlamaqui names Grotius for the division of justice into expletive and attributive, which is defined at I.i.8.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui makes Barbeyrac's argument against those who undermine reason, with the same Romans 2:14-15 proof in shared non-biblical wording ('les commandemens de la Loi sont écrits dans leurs cœurs').

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same rejection of natural law's co-eternity with God on the ground that it is made for men and its actual existence presupposes them, with shared key words.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: The footnote names Grotius I.1 § 10, the section whose opening this is.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Near-identical clause limiting liberty to acts the soul can suspend or turn as it pleases.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The ceteris-paribus self-preservation maxim matches, but Pufendorf's passage is about dying for others; Burlamaqui's conflict rule is near-verbatim from Barbeyrac's note in the Droit de la nature, not this passage.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Burlamaqui cites Pufendorf I.6.4 and openly judges his definition of law too vague and too narrow.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same concession that wrong actions may 'procurer quelque plaisir/avantage', answered with 'outre que' and their short duration, but the rest of the content differs, so 'loose paraphrase' fits better.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The example of a man who marries another's wife, believing her unmarried or her husband dead, as essential error is copied word for word from Barbeyrac's Devoirs note.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Close restatement of Pufendorf's sentence on self-love: seeking self-preservation by all means, pursuing the good and fleeing the bad.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: The note prints Cicero's Latin sentence word for word with its reference; for this Latin passage the relation is verbatim quotation, not translation.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The criticism of the distributive/permutative subdivision is copied almost word for word from Barbeyrac's note.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's specific example of a loaded pistol left on a table where a child is hurt, with the same responsibility conclusion, in closely parallel sentences.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same distinction of antecedent and subsequent conscience, with the same clause 'ou avant que de les faire, ou après les avoir faites'.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The antecedent/subsequent division of conscience is a stock scholastic distinction, and this note only reports the original's terms (with 'conséquente', not Burlamaqui's 'subséquente'), so nothing ties Burlamaqui to this passage in particular.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's own PDP repeats the PDN claim that laws reach inner actions and thoughts, with the same 'autant du moins que' restriction.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument and near-identical wording from Pufendorf: it is not beyond human firmness to suffer death, so one can be bound to it rather than fail in duty.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same remark, in parallel wording, that the desire for immortality grows as one cultivates reason, within the same proof.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui reuses Barbeyrac's note: a person acting under threat 'concourt en quelque maniere a l'action visiblement mauvaise' and acts with a kind of will.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Note (b) expressly cites Grotius II.20.19, which is the passage on faults due to human frailty.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The principle is in identical words, and Burlamaqui's section on imputing others' actions follows Pufendorf's Devoirs.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The definition of human actions, as depending on the soul in origin or direction, and the inference that the soul is their principle are nearly word for word in both texts.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument in the same form: natural law or obligation is universal because all men are subject to God's empire.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same citation of Bernard, Nouv. de la Rép. des Lettres, Aug. 1702, p. 211, with the same remark about the pleasure of copying his judicious reflections.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui takes Pufendorf I.7.2's sequence: one is indispensably obliged by the superior, and jurisconsults speak of forbidden acts as impossible though physically possible.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Same example of marrying another's wife and the same clause 'qui regarde la nature même de la chose, & qui est par conséquent essentielle'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's argument that marking the bounds of obligation thereby fixes a positive permission (Selden's boundary image) is restated; the exact wording is in Barbeyrac's note on Grotius I.1.9.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Burlamaqui quotes and credits the stock Terence line; nothing ties it to Seneca's use of it.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Both of Burlamaqui's texts give the same definition of the good or just action as one 'exactement conforme' to the law.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's note names Hutcheson ('Mr. Hutchinson') for the term moral sense, which the Inquiry sets out in Treatise II sect. 1.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's note (a) cites Pufendorf I.1 §19 for listing power along with right among moral qualities.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Definition of invincible error taken from Pufendorf I.3.11: 'se garantir', 'tous les soins moralement possibles', glossed by the constitution of human things.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note on doubtful conscience, like Burlamaqui's rule, says acting in doubt exposes one to error and that this holds 'sur tout dans les choses de grande importance'.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's note cites Leibniz's Jugement and Barbeyrac's remarks joined to the Devoirs, not Barbeyrac's Grotius; this source is not named, only the same reflections are mentioned in both.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Verbatim proviso that the incapacity must not be self-inflicted, followed by the Roman thumb-cutting example from Barbeyrac's note.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same definition of man as an animal endowed with intelligence and reason, composed of body and soul, in near-identical words.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Burlamaqui names Barbeyrac's notes on the cited passages and adopts this note's view that permission is a positive, tacit act, not a mere inaction.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui quotes in guillemets Pufendorf's report of the view that power gives the right to reign by making resistance impossible, nearly word for word.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: The footnote names Grotius I.1.3 for jus rectorium and aequatorium, the superior/equal division in the source.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's collateral causes repeat Grotius II.21.1's list of accomplices, those who furnish help to the doer or give him refuge, almost word for word.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same sentence frame and argument against Hobbes: whoever alleges only superior force has no ground to oblige.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: The note names Grotius I.1 § 9, the passage where permission is called a mere inaction of the law.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui takes Barbeyrac's proposed term 'imparfaite ou non rigoureuse' (the same note also supplies the rest of § XI), but builds a different sentence around it.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: The clause is verbatim and the context continues with Hobbes's division and 'dénomination extérieure', as in Pufendorf II.3.23.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note argues against Pufendorf that there are degrees of vice as of virtue and probity; Burlamaqui makes the same point in the same pairing of terms.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The two Burlamaqui texts share the definition of vincible error as error contracted by negligence, avoidable with all the attention one was capable of, in nearly the same words.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The end of the Seneca quotation follows Barbeyrac's French wording phrase by phrase (remedies, help in old age, defying Fortune, 'Otez la Sociabilité...').

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both versions of the conscience chapter open on the point that law serves as rule or binds only when known, and go on to conscience as the immediate rule; shared passage in other words.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's rule for doubtful cases (principal vs subordinate or collateral causes) repeats Barbeyrac's note almost word for word.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Imputation to superiors who neglected the care required by 'la nature & l'étendue de son pouvoir' follows Pufendorf's wording closely.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The invincible-ignorance rule is near verbatim, and the following lines on the possibility of instruction in ordinary life also match.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same definition of essential error, with the same structure and closing clause about its influence on the action taken.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That fear does not excuse breaking a strict duty is the standard doctrine on constrained actions; Barbeyrac's side-remark in a note on promises is not specifically Burlamaqui's source.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both texts treat the end of law separately with respect to subjects and to the sovereign.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same question in the same structure and mostly the same words (body's death/dissolution necessarily brings the soul's annihilation), followed in both by the argument that the body itself is not annihilated.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: They share only the stock Burlamaqui phrase 'un être intelligent et libre'. The PDN point (moral necessity leaves freedom intact) and the PDP point (man acts on his judgments) are not the same argument.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui follows Pufendorf I.9.3's contrast between rewards that can be claimed and penalties 'décernées' for bad actions, which he expands with Barbeyrac's note.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui applies Barbeyrac's distinction between imputability and actual imputation, the latter requiring an obligation to act or abstain, to coerced acts.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The exposure of children by Greeks and Romans is a commonplace example; Locke uses it against innate principles, Burlamaqui as an error of law, and his note cites Matthew, not Locke.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Only the stock pairing praise/blame, reward/punishment is shared; the Principes speak of their degrees, the Elemens of the two modes of imputation.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both say the punishing authority may pardon, a commonplace, but the PDP passage is about the transfer of the right to punish to the magistrate, not the legislator's discretion over the sanction.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both use the stock argument that matter at rest cannot move itself and needs an outside first mover, but the fragments state different propositions and share no wording.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's second natural law presupposing a human establishment such as property matches Grotius's law of nature that supposes a certain state of things, and note (a) cites Grotius I.1 § 10.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's division into obligatory law and law 'de simple permission' takes Barbeyrac's specific pairing of a natural law of simple permission beside an obligatory one.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The Locke source passage is a fragment, and deceptive appearances of good and evil are a commonplace; nothing specific links Burlamaqui to this Locke section.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui says himself that everyone agrees God's will is the source of obligation; nothing ties his sentence to Barbeyrac's note in particular.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Mind moving the body at its pleasure is a dualist commonplace, and Burlamaqui uses it to argue the soul is spiritual, which Locke's passage does not do.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's definition of law as a notified will, with the form of notification indifferent, follows Barbeyrac's note saying notification need not be by words or writing.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Penalty as threatened and then actually inflicted is the stock idea of sanction; the Devoirs passage justifies penal power and is not Burlamaqui's definition.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui echoes Leibniz's sequence: principles so simple that subtle minds sought novel paradoxes, against the fecundity of the simple ones.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That a wise being proposes an end and uses the necessary means is a stock idea, and nothing ties Burlamaqui's sentence to Cumberland's phrase.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The observation that good men suffer like others is a commonplace, and the two works put it to different uses.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both say injustice's gains, whatever passing success they bring, are not solid or lasting, but this is a moral commonplace, the contexts differ (sanction against utility debate), and the wording is not specific.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both explain away savage peoples' apparent lack of moral notions by their brutishness, but only the word 'abruti' is shared and this reply to the Lockean objection is common stock.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same sentence on the lawgiver's own end (satisfaction and glory) in both Burlamaqui texts.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Same debate on whether relations in the nature of things oblige, but this passage only states the rationalist view that Barbeyrac rejects; Burlamaqui answers Barbeyrac's claim later in the chapter.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The phrase 'gêner la liberté des sujets' recurs, but this Élémens sentence belongs to the end-of-law discussion (parallel of § III), and the Élémens' own parallel for the utility condition is a different sentence.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's 'hors de la Société, il ne sauroit ni conserver sa vie, ni ...' reworks Pufendorf's step from man's inability to survive without others ('il ne sauroit subsister, ni jouïr des biens ... s'il n'est sociable') to sociability.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's definition of imputation follows Pufendorf I.5.3: the author or moral cause, good or bad effects attributed to him, and responsibility.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The Principes and the Élémens share the clause on holding life, reason and all advantages from God, in the same structure and nearly the same words.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Only the stock formula of what one 'could and should' prevent is shared, used for different questions (imputing others' acts vs damage by omission).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both of Burlamaqui's texts end the account of the faculties the same way: the faculties joined together lead to knowledge of truth and then to true happiness.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The Elemens line is the definition of droit (parallel to Principes I.5.10); P2.8.3 only restates the same doctrine that reason approves what leads to happiness.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both treat the guilt of accomplices, but the Principes says a plot makes all ordinarily equally guilty while the Droit politique punishes each in proportion to his share.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both say mental faculties are unequal in degree among men, but this is a commonplace and the shared wording is minimal.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both derive the general principles of natural law from the same three states of man, Burlamaqui's own scheme in the parallel chapter.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same author and place: God's existence is a truth evident from all sides, with clear and convincing proofs; the Principes expand the Élémens sentence.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The PDP sentence is a narrower case (a law forbidding even the thought) within the parallel section; only the general point that law reaches thoughts links it to this passage.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Only the generic phrase 'faire un juste discernement' of goods and evils is shared; nothing specific ties Burlamaqui's rule to Pouilly.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pouilly's 'joye secrette toujours prete à se developer' (ch. XVI) describes the contentment of people in moderate labour, not the joy that follows a good action; only the phrase is shared.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both texts give Burlamaqui's own definition of obligation as a restriction of liberty produced by reason.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That society cannot subsist without abstaining from harm is a commonplace; nothing specific links Burlamaqui's summary to this sentence of the Devoirs.
